/-!
# Dirac–Motzkin conjecture

Let $P$ be a finite set of $n$ points in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, not all on one
line. A line is *ordinary* (for $P$) if it contains exactly two points of $P$. The
Sylvester–Gallai theorem says that $P$ spans at least one ordinary line. The Dirac–Motzkin
conjecture (Dirac, 1951) states that $P$ always spans at least $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ ordinary
lines.

The bound is attained for all even $n > 4$ by constructions of Böröczky, and for odd $n$ by the
Kelly–Moser configuration ($n = 7$, three ordinary lines) and the McKee configuration ($n = 13$,
six ordinary lines). Green and Tao [GT13] proved the conjecture for all sufficiently large $n$
(in the stronger form "at least $n/2$ ordinary lines"); for general $n$ it remains open.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Sylvester–Gallai theorem, *The number of ordinary lines*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvester%E2%80%93Gallai_theorem%23The_number_of_ordinary_lines)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [GT13] Green, B., Tao, T. *On sets defining few ordinary lines*. Discrete Comput. Geom. 50
  (2013). [arXiv:1208.4714](https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.4714)
-/

justification.closest_existing_considered: `Collinear ℝ` / `EuclideanGeometry.NonTrilinear` / `NonCollinearFor` (FormalConjecturesForMathlib/Geometry/2d.lean) express collinearity constraints but do not count lines; the private `Erdos101.linesWithPointsFor k S` has the same shape but is inaccessible.

justification.why_needed: Neither Mathlib nor FormalConjecturesForMathlib has a notion of 'lines determined by a point set containing exactly k points of it'. The only nearby idiom (`linesWithPointsFor` in FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/101.lean) is `private` and thus not reusable. The definition is the set of lines `line[ℝ, p, q]` spanned by distinct p, q ∈ P whose intersection with P has ncard 2. theorem ordinaryLines_finite {P : Set ℝ²} (hP : P.Finite) : (ordinaryLines P).Finite := by

@[category test, AMS 51 52]
theorem mem_ordinaryLines_pair {p q : ℝ²} (hpq : p ≠ q) :
    line[ℝ, p, q] ∈ ordinaryLines {p, q} := by
  refine ⟨p, by simp, q, by simp, hpq, rfl, ?_⟩
  rw [Set.inter_eq_right.mpr, Set.ncard_pair hpq]
  rintro x (rfl | rfl)
  · exact left_mem_affineSpan_pair ℝ _ _
  · exact right_mem_affineSpan_pair ℝ _ _

@[category test, AMS 51 52]
theorem ordinaryLines_eq_empty_of_collinear (S : Finset ℝ²) (hS : Collinear ℝ (S : Set ℝ²))
    (hcard : 3 ≤ S.card) : ordinaryLines S = ∅ := by
  ext L
  simp only [ordinaryLines, Set.mem_setOf_eq, Set.mem_empty_iff_false, iff_false]
  rintro ⟨p, hp, q, hq, hpq, rfl, h2⟩
  have hsub : (S : Set ℝ²) ⊆ (line[ℝ, p, q] : Set ℝ²) := fun r hr =>
    hS.mem_affineSpan_of_mem_of_ne hp hq hr hpq
  rw [Set.inter_eq_right.mpr hsub, Set.ncard_coe_finset] at h2
  omega

@[category research open, AMS 51 52]
theorem dirac_motzkin_conjecture (P : Finset ℝ²) (hP : ¬ Collinear ℝ (P : Set ℝ²)) :
    P.card / 2 ≤ (ordinaryLines P).ncard := by
  sorry
blocks.docstring:
**Dirac–Motzkin conjecture.** Every finite set $P$ of $n$ points in the Euclidean plane
$\mathbb{R}^2$, not all on one line, spans at least $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ ordinary lines, that is,
lines containing exactly two points of $P$. Here `P.card / 2` is natural number division, so it
equals $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$.

The hypothesis that the points are not all collinear excludes the degenerate case of a
collinear set, which spans no ordinary line at all; in particular it forces $n \geq 3$.
The floor is essential: the Kelly–Moser configuration ($n = 7$) has exactly $3$ ordinary lines
and the McKee configuration ($n = 13$) has exactly $6$.

claims.decomposer_note: Per the article, the conjecture is: every finite set of n points in ℝ², not all collinear, spans at least ⌊n/2⌋ ordinary lines (lines containing exactly two of the points), for all n; note the floor — the Kelly–Moser (n=7, 3 lines) and McKee (n=13, 6 lines) configurations attain equality rather than refuting it, whereas Green–Tao's 'at least n/2' phrasing is strictly stronger for odd n, fails at n=7,13, and is only proved/conjectured for n ≥ n₀ (possibly n₀=14); the non-collinearity hypothesis (and hence n ≥ 3) is essential to exclude the degenerate case with zero ordinary lines.
claims.reviewer_why: All eight candidates state the same faithful proposition: for every P : Finset ℝ² with ¬ Collinear ℝ ↑P, P.card / 2 ≤ #(ordinary lines of P), where ordinary lines are the affine lines line[ℝ,p,q] (p ≠ q ∈ P) meeting P in exactly two points (c08 equivalently uses finrank-1 affine subspaces meeting S in exactly 2 points). This matches the cited Wikipedia section verbatim ('Dirac (1951) conjectured t₂(n) ≥ ⌊n/2⌋ for all n ... often referred to as the Dirac–Motzkin conjecture'). Checks: ℕ-division gives the floor (Kelly–Moser n=7 and McKee n=13 attain equality, not refute); ¬Collinear excludes the degenerate collinear case and forces n ≥ 3 since ∅/singletons/pairs are Collinear in Mathlib; lines are counted as AffineSubspace values so each geometric line is counted once; the set of ordinary lines is provably finite (API lemma included), so Set.ncard is the genuine count; quantifier order ∀P is correct and the hypothesis is satisfiable (any triangle). c07 chosen as base for its clean Set-based bespoke definition, proven finiteness/API tests and clear docstrings; I added c05's proven test that a collinear set of ≥3 points has no ordinary lines (documenting the role of the hypothesis), and dropped the non-slot Green–Tao/Kelly–Moser/Csima–Sawyer variants so the file contains exactly the adjudicated slot.

context:
The Sylvester–Gallai theorem in geometry states that every finite set of points in the Euclidean plane has a line that passes through exactly two of the points or a line that passes through all of them. It is named after James Joseph Sylvester, who posed it as a problem in 1893, and Tibor Gallai, who published one of the first proofs of this theorem in 1944.
A line that contains exactly two of a set of points is known as an ordinary line. Another way of stating the theorem is that every finite set of points that is not collinear has an ordinary line. According to a strengthening of the theorem, every finite point set (not all on one line) has at least a linear number of ordinary lines. An algorithm can find an ordinary line in a set of $n$ points in time $O(n\log n)$.

decomposition_objections.text: None. The table's single slot and its notes (floor, non-collinearity hypothesis, contrast with Green–Tao's n/2 phrasing) agree with the Wikipedia section and the Green–Tao paper; the file follows them exactly.

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Dirac–Motzkin conjecture

Let $P$ be a finite set of $n$ points in the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$, not all on one
line. A line is *ordinary* (for $P$) if it contains exactly two points of $P$. The
Sylvester–Gallai theorem says that $P$ spans at least one ordinary line. The Dirac–Motzkin
conjecture (Dirac, 1951) states that $P$ always spans at least $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ ordinary
lines.

The bound is attained for all even $n > 4$ by constructions of Böröczky, and for odd $n$ by the
Kelly–Moser configuration ($n = 7$, three ordinary lines) and the McKee configuration ($n = 13$,
six ordinary lines). Green and Tao [GT13] proved the conjecture for all sufficiently large $n$
(in the stronger form "at least $n/2$ ordinary lines"); for general $n$ it remains open.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Sylvester–Gallai theorem, *The number of ordinary lines*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sylvester%E2%80%93Gallai_theorem%23The_number_of_ordinary_lines)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- [GT13] Green, B., Tao, T. *On sets defining few ordinary lines*. Discrete Comput. Geom. 50
  (2013). [arXiv:1208.4714](https://arxiv.org/abs/1208.4714)
-/

namespace DiracMotzkinConjecture

open EuclideanGeometry

/--
The set of *ordinary lines* of a set `P` of points in the plane: the lines spanned by two
distinct points of `P` that contain exactly two points of `P`. Lines are represented as affine
subspaces of `ℝ²`.
-/
def ordinaryLines (P : Set ℝ²) : Set (AffineSubspace ℝ ℝ²) :=
  {L | ∃ p ∈ P, ∃ q ∈ P, p ≠ q ∧ L = line[ℝ, p, q] ∧ (↑L ∩ P).ncard = 2}

/-- A finite set of points has finitely many ordinary lines. -/
@[category API, AMS 51 52]
theorem ordinaryLines_finite {P : Set ℝ²} (hP : P.Finite) : (ordinaryLines P).Finite := by
  refine ((hP.prod hP).image fun pq ↦ line[ℝ, pq.1, pq.2]).subset ?_
  rintro L ⟨p, hp, q, hq, -, rfl, -⟩
  exact ⟨(p, q), ⟨hp, hq⟩, rfl⟩

/-- The line through two distinct points is an ordinary line of the pair. -/
@[category test, AMS 51 52]
theorem mem_ordinaryLines_pair {p q : ℝ²} (hpq : p ≠ q) :
    line[ℝ, p, q] ∈ ordinaryLines {p, q} := by
  refine ⟨p, by simp, q, by simp, hpq, rfl, ?_⟩
  rw [Set.inter_eq_right.mpr, Set.ncard_pair hpq]
  rintro x (rfl | rfl)
  · exact left_mem_affineSpan_pair ℝ _ _
  · exact right_mem_affineSpan_pair ℝ _ _

/-- The empty set of points has no ordinary lines. -/
@[category test, AMS 51 52]
theorem ordinaryLines_empty : ordinaryLines ∅ = ∅ := by
  ext L
  simp [ordinaryLines]

/-- A set of at least three collinear points spans no ordinary line. This is the degenerate
case excluded by the hypothesis of the Dirac–Motzkin conjecture. -/
@[category test, AMS 51 52]
theorem ordinaryLines_eq_empty_of_collinear (S : Finset ℝ²) (hS : Collinear ℝ (S : Set ℝ²))
    (hcard : 3 ≤ S.card) : ordinaryLines S = ∅ := by
  ext L
  simp only [ordinaryLines, Set.mem_setOf_eq, Set.mem_empty_iff_false, iff_false]
  rintro ⟨p, hp, q, hq, hpq, rfl, h2⟩
  have hsub : (S : Set ℝ²) ⊆ (line[ℝ, p, q] : Set ℝ²) := fun r hr =>
    hS.mem_affineSpan_of_mem_of_ne hp hq hr hpq
  rw [Set.inter_eq_right.mpr hsub, Set.ncard_coe_finset] at h2
  omega

/--
**Dirac–Motzkin conjecture.** Every finite set $P$ of $n$ points in the Euclidean plane
$\mathbb{R}^2$, not all on one line, spans at least $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ ordinary lines, that is,
lines containing exactly two points of $P$. Here `P.card / 2` is natural number division, so it
equals $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$.

The hypothesis that the points are not all collinear excludes the degenerate case of a
collinear set, which spans no ordinary line at all; in particular it forces $n \geq 3$.
The floor is essential: the Kelly–Moser configuration ($n = 7$) has exactly $3$ ordinary lines
and the McKee configuration ($n = 13$) has exactly $6$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51 52]
theorem dirac_motzkin_conjecture (P : Finset ℝ²) (hP : ¬ Collinear ℝ (P : Set ℝ²)) :
    P.card / 2 ≤ (ordinaryLines P).ncard := by
  sorry

end DiracMotzkinConjecture

items: The list-page entry is terse; the precise formulation was taken from the linked Wikipedia section: every set of n points in ℝ², not all on one line, spans at least ⌊n/2⌋ ordinary lines. The floor (Dirac's form) is used, not Green–Tao's 'n/2' form; the latter is included separately as `dirac_motzkin_conjecture.variants.green_tao` (category research solved, ∃ n₀ threshold, real division), matching Green–Tao Theorem 1.2.

Points are modeled as `Finset ℝ²` with `ℝ² = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)` (repo's scoped notation); 'not all collinear' is `¬ Collinear ℝ (P : Set ℝ²)`. Since sets of ≤ 2 points are collinear in Mathlib, this excludes n ≤ 2 and the hypothesis is satisfiable (e.g. a triangle).

Ordinary lines are modeled as elements of `Set (AffineSubspace ℝ ℝ²)`: `L ∈ ordinaryLines P ↔ ∃ p q ∈ P, p ≠ q ∧ L = line[ℝ, p, q] ∧ (↑L ∩ P).ncard = 2`. Counting affine subspaces (rather than pairs of points) means each geometric line is counted once. This is equivalent to Wikipedia's 'a line that contains exactly two of the points', since any line through two points of P is spanned by them.
The number of ordinary lines is `Set.ncard`; the API lemma `ordinaryLines_finite` proves the set is finite for finite P, so `ncard` is the genuine cardinality (no infinite-set default 0 issue).

⌊n/2⌋ is written as `P.card / 2` (ℕ floor division), with non-strict `≤`, so the Kelly–Moser (n=7, 3 lines) and McKee (n=13, 6 lines) configurations attain equality rather than contradict the statement.
